Education in Entrepreneurship: Necessary or Antiquated?

Everyone and their mother seems to be “working on a startup” these days. Maybe there’s something appealing about the idea of being your own boss, working your own hours, and not having to answer to “The Man.” Some may call it escaping the system, others may call it running to another. Regardless of your views on this renewed entrepreneurial spirit that perhaps subsists a little bit too much on dropshipping and course-selling and not enough on educational attainment followed by its application, it is undeniably shaping the future in ways that are not yet measurable With high-school-aged influencers on social media flaunting stacks of cash and fancy sports cars, the narrative being pushed on us seems to be that education does not equal success (at least when you can sell your fitness course online for $15 a customer). So the question follows: for those of us with that… hustler instinct, what is the right next step? If these adolescents can make more money in a month than the average American does in a year without ever seeing the front side of a degree (other than the one hanging in their high school principal’s office), it makes you wonder where all that tuition money went. Is education no longer a necessary feature for entrepreneurial success? Or is it time to assuage these anti-education sentiments? The answer, it seems, is that it depends.

The figure below depicts data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor,1 which interviews over 100,000 entrepreneurs across the globe yearly.

We can see in the depiction the average education level of entrepreneurs per country measured against the average perceived ease of starting a business. The entrepreneurs in countries that appear higher on the graph on average believe it easier to start a business, and the entrepreneurs in countries to the right are generally more educated. At first glance, there seems to be no apparent relationship between education and ease of starting a business. We can actually confirm this by calculating the correlation between education and perceived ease of starting a business, which comes out to 0.012. This correlation indicates an essentially negligible relationship between education and perceived ease. It would seem from this that the more educated an individual is, does not necessarily translate to how easy it would be for them to start a business.

If we take a look, though, at the countries highlighted in red, we see an interesting result. According to Pitchbook data,2 these countries are home to the top 100 entrepreneur-producing schools globally. Yet, there still seems to be no visible correlation. It seems that when we control for education, we still can’t account for the varied ease of starting a business. Education seems to help in some cases, and it doesn’t seem to do anything in others.

Some people may be convinced at this point. All points seem to lead to the fact that education has no effect on the behavior of entrepreneurs. After all, don’t they always say it’s who you know, not what you know? Let’s look at the graph below and see if that’s really true.

This graph depicts the average network of entrepreneurs across the globe, on a scale of “none” to “few” to “many.” Bars highlighted green are above the 50th percentile in terms of entrepreneurial ease. If networking had anything to do with how easy it becomes to start a business, we would expect to see some sort of clustering of green to the right. Yet, look at the graph, we still see green staggered throughout the entire depiction, indicating that it is not in fact who you know. A larger network does not correlate to how easy it is for them to start a business.

In addition, returning to the Pitchbook Top 100, we can see that the countries (in red) that produce the most successful entrepreneurs do not show any correlation at all between network and success. They are grouped mainly, even, to the left! It seems counterintuitive that neither education nor networks display any effect on entrepreneurial success, or the ease of starting a business. But, maybe that’s the point.

In both charts above, I want to highlight in particular the countries of Israel (IL), South Africa (ZA), and South Korea (KR). Israel, one of the most highly educated countries, also seems to be one of the ones in which it is hardest to start a business. And yet, as seen in the table below, it has eight (eight!) schools on the Pitchbook Top 100 list. South Africa and South Korea, two of the most poorly connected countries according to the GEM dataset, both contain schools in the Pitchbook Top 100! How could this be?

It seems that no matter what metric you’re accounting for, whether it be education level or networking opportunities, there is no surefire easy pathway to success as an entrepreneur. You could have the top education in the world, or be connected with the top business minds in the country, and that still doesn’t make entrepreneurship easy. And the opposite is true as well. Countries with poor education, or with relatively few connections, still come out on top with some of the leading entrepreneurial endeavors across the globe.

It’s hard for many, but that shouldn’t stop you. So the question we asked in the beginning: is education important for entrepreneurial success? The answer seems to be that there’s no way to tell. And it doesn’t really matter. The real measure of success, regardless of difficulty or education or network or the lack thereof, is just a matter of effort. Anyone can do it, and that’s the whole beauty of it. That’s part of the reason why so many people are turning to entrepreneurship so early. It doesn’t mean you have to drop out of school and throw your degree in the garbage; it just means that you can disregard what everyone else is doing, because the ultimate measure of success isn’t the school name on your diploma or the number of connections you have on LinkedIn. It’s you.

Methodological Appendix

This analysis uses data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) Adult Population Survey, which surveys over 100,000 individuals annually across more than 50 countries. The dataset includes individual-level measures of education (GEMEDUC), perceived ease of starting a business (easystartL, measured on a 1–5 scale), and entrepreneurial networking (knowentR), along with country-specific survey weights. All statistics were calculated using these weights to ensure nationally representative estimates. Individual responses were aggregated to the country level by computing weighted means for each variable, producing a cross-national dataset of average entrepreneurial characteristics by country.

To contextualize these outcomes within elite educational environments, an external dataset from Pitchbook’s Top 100 Entrepreneur-Producing Universities rankings was incorporated. This dataset was aggregated to the country level by counting the number of top-ranked institutions per country. Countries appearing in the Pitchbook rankings were flagged as “Top Schools” and used solely for annotation and subgroup comparison in visualizations. No individual-level linkage between the GEM and Pitchbook data was performed; the Pitchbook data serve as a country-level indicator of entrepreneurial prestige rather than a direct measure of educational attainment.

The analytical approach relies on weighted descriptive analysis and correlation estimation rather than causal inference. A custom weighted Pearson correlation was calculated between education and perceived ease of starting a business to account for population size and sampling design. Visualizations, including scatter plots and ordered bar charts, were used to examine whether education levels or entrepreneurial networks cluster with higher perceived ease across countries. Countries were binned using median splits for ease of interpretation, and color highlighting was applied to identify high-ease countries and those with top entrepreneur-producing universities. This approach allows technically informed readers to reproduce the analysis directly using publicly available GEM data and standard statistical software.
